reason: The text consistently employs national and collective terminology for the Israelites: עֲדַת בְּנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל ('congregation of Israel') describes an organized collective body, בְּנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל ('Israelites') designates them as a distinct people with national identity, and הָעָם ('the people') emphasizes their status as a unified populace. Critically, the text references זִקְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל ('elders of Israel'), indicating governmental and organizational structures beyond familial bonds. The narrative depicts them undertaking coordinated national movement (וַיִּסְעוּ כָּל־עֲדַת - 'the entire congregation journeyed'), collective settlement, and unified grievances against leadership—all attributes of a nation-state rather than a kinship group or religious sect. While theocratic elements are present (Yahweh's direction), the portrayal emphasizes their status as an organized people and nation with internal political structure.
